First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis

Author

Davin Cuaso

Published

6 September 2026

Modified

12 September 2026

Overview

This exercise follows Chapter 4: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis and studies the distribution of childcare services in Singapore. It answers two questions:

  1. Are childcare centres consistent with complete spatial randomness (CSR)?
  2. Where is first-order intensity highest, and how sensitive is it to bandwidth choice?

Data and point-pattern preparation

Dataset Source Use
Child Care Services ECDA via data.gov.sg Point events
Master Plan 2019 Planning Area Boundary (No Sea) URA via data.gov.sg Observation window and comparisons

Distance-based analysis requires metres, so both layers are transformed to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414). The union of all planning areas becomes the polygonal observation window.

Show the R code 
planning_area <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MP2019_PlanningArea.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(3414)

childcare <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "ChildCareServices.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(3414)

singapore_window <- as.owin(st_union(planning_area))
xy <- st_coordinates(childcare)

childcare_ppp <- ppp(
  x = xy[, 1],
  y = xy[, 2],
  window = singapore_window,
  checkdup = FALSE
)

pattern_summary <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Childcare centres", "Planning areas", "Projected CRS", "Observation-window area (km²)"),
  Value = c(
    npoints(childcare_ppp),
    nrow(planning_area),
    st_crs(childcare)$epsg,
    round(area.owin(singapore_window) / 1e6, 1)
  )
)
kable(pattern_summary, caption = "Validated point-pattern inputs")
Validated point-pattern inputs
Measure Value
Childcare centres 1925.0
Planning areas 55.0
Projected CRS 3414.0
Observation-window area (km²) 784.9
Show the R code 
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = planning_area, fill = "#f5f7fa", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = childcare, color = "#c43c39", size = 0.35, alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Childcare centres follow Singapore's populated urban footprint",
    subtitle = paste(format(nrow(childcare), big.mark = ","), "service locations")
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test

The null hypothesis is CSR. Values of the Clark–Evans ratio (R<1) indicate shorter nearest-neighbour distances than expected under CSR; (R>1) indicates a more regular pattern. The CDF edge correction is suitable for the non-rectangular Singapore window.

Show the R code 
ce_sg <- clarkevans.test(
  childcare_ppp,
  correction = "cdf",
  alternative = "clustered"
)

ce_result <- data.frame(
  Area = "Singapore",
  `Clark-Evans R` = round(unname(ce_sg$statistic), 3),
  `p-value` = format.pval(ce_sg$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
  Decision = ifelse(ce_sg$p.value < 0.05, "Reject CSR", "Do not reject CSR"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(ce_result, caption = "Clark–Evans test with CDF edge correction")
Clark–Evans test with CDF edge correction
Area Clark-Evans R p-value Decision
Singapore 0.486 <0.001 Reject CSR

Answer. (R=) 0.486 with < 0.001, so the childcare pattern is significantly clustered relative to CSR. This is not evidence that centres attract one another; population, housing estates, zoning, and service demand are plausible spatially varying drivers.

Kernel density estimation

bw.diggle() selects a data-driven fixed bandwidth. An adaptive KDE is also estimated: it uses narrower kernels where points are dense and wider kernels in sparse areas. Both surfaces are expressed as estimated centres per square kilometre.

Show the R code 
fixed_bandwidth <- bw.diggle(childcare_ppp)

fixed_kde <- density(
  childcare_ppp,
  sigma = fixed_bandwidth,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

adaptive_kde <- adaptive.density(
  childcare_ppp,
  f = 0.15,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

fixed_grid <- as.data.frame(fixed_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = paste0("Fixed KDE (h = ", round(fixed_bandwidth), " m)"))

adaptive_grid <- as.data.frame(adaptive_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = "Adaptive KDE")

kde_grid <- bind_rows(fixed_grid, adaptive_grid)
Show the R code 
ggplot(kde_grid, aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = planning_area, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.08, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(planning_area), datum = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", trans = "sqrt", na.value = NA) +
  labs(
    fill = "Estimated centres\nper km²",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

Answer. The fixed-bandwidth surface peaks in Sengkang. The fixed surface is easier to compare across the island; the adaptive surface retains sharper local peaks in dense estates and smooths more aggressively in sparse peripheral areas. KDE measures concentration of facilities, not accessibility or demand satisfaction.

Planning-area comparison

The course guide compares Punggol, Tampines, Choa Chu Kang, and Jurong West. Counts and area-standardised densities show why raw totals alone can mislead.

Show the R code 
focus_names <- c("PUNGGOL", "TAMPINES", "CHOA CHU KANG", "JURONG WEST")

childcare_with_area <- st_join(
  childcare,
  planning_area["PLN_AREA_N"],
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE
)

focus_summary <- planning_area |>
  filter(PLN_AREA_N %in% focus_names) |>
  mutate(Area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(PLN_AREA_N, Area_km2) |>
  left_join(
    childcare_with_area |>
      st_drop_geometry() |>
      count(PLN_AREA_N, name = "Centres"),
    by = "PLN_AREA_N"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `Centres per km²` = Centres / Area_km2,
    Area_km2 = round(Area_km2, 2),
    `Centres per km²` = round(`Centres per km²`, 2)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(`Centres per km²`))

kable(
  focus_summary,
  col.names = c("Planning area", "Area (km²)", "Centres", "Centres per km²"),
  caption = "Childcare provision in the four focus planning areas"
)
Childcare provision in the four focus planning areas
Planning area Area (km²) Centres Centres per km²
CHOA CHU KANG 6.12 74 12.10
PUNGGOL 9.37 72 7.68
JURONG WEST 14.68 110 7.49
TAMPINES 20.80 117 5.63
Show the R code 
make_local_ppp <- function(area_name) {
  boundary <- planning_area |> filter(PLN_AREA_N == area_name)
  local_points <- childcare[lengths(st_within(childcare, boundary)) > 0, ]
  local_xy <- st_coordinates(local_points)
  ppp(
    local_xy[, 1], local_xy[, 2],
    window = as.owin(st_union(boundary)),
    checkdup = FALSE
  )
}

local_tests <- lapply(c("CHOA CHU KANG", "TAMPINES"), function(area_name) {
  local_ppp <- make_local_ppp(area_name)
  test <- clarkevans.test(local_ppp, correction = "cdf", alternative = "clustered")
  data.frame(
    `Planning area` = tools::toTitleCase(tolower(area_name)),
    Centres = npoints(local_ppp),
    `Clark-Evans R` = round(unname(test$statistic), 3),
    `p-value` = format.pval(test$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()

kable(local_tests, caption = "Local Clark–Evans tests")
Local Clark–Evans tests
Planning area Centres Clark-Evans R p-value
Choa Chu Kang 74 0.794 <0.001
Tampines 117 0.663 <0.001

Tampines has more centres, while Choa Chu Kang has greater centres-per-area density because its boundary is much smaller. Both local (R) values are below 1 and statistically significant, so clustering is present within each planning area rather than being only an island-wide effect.

Conclusion

The nearest-neighbour and KDE results agree: childcare services are not distributed uniformly. The strongest fixed-KDE concentration is in Sengkang, and substantial local clustering remains in Choa Chu Kang and Tampines. These are descriptive first-order findings; a demand-adjusted study would add child population, capacity, transport access, and housing density.

## Overview

This exercise follows [Chapter 4: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap04.html) and studies the distribution of childcare services in Singapore. It answers two questions:

1. Are childcare centres consistent with complete spatial randomness (CSR)?
2. Where is first-order intensity highest, and how sensitive is it to bandwidth choice?

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(spatstat.geom)
library(spatstat.explore)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
options(scipen = 999)
data_path <- "../../data"
```

## Data and point-pattern preparation

| Dataset | Source | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Child Care Services | [ECDA via data.gov.sg](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_5d668e3f544335f8028f546827b773b4/view) | Point events |
| Master Plan 2019 Planning Area Boundary (No Sea) | [URA via data.gov.sg](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_4765db0e87b9c86336792efe8a1f7a66/view) | Observation window and comparisons |

Distance-based analysis requires metres, so both layers are transformed to **SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414)**. The union of all planning areas becomes the polygonal observation window.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-point-pattern

planning_area <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MP2019_PlanningArea.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(3414)

childcare <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "ChildCareServices.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(3414)

singapore_window <- as.owin(st_union(planning_area))
xy <- st_coordinates(childcare)

childcare_ppp <- ppp(
  x = xy[, 1],
  y = xy[, 2],
  window = singapore_window,
  checkdup = FALSE
)

pattern_summary <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Childcare centres", "Planning areas", "Projected CRS", "Observation-window area (km²)"),
  Value = c(
    npoints(childcare_ppp),
    nrow(planning_area),
    st_crs(childcare)$epsg,
    round(area.owin(singapore_window) / 1e6, 1)
  )
)
kable(pattern_summary, caption = "Validated point-pattern inputs")
```

```{r}
#| label: event-map
#| fig-cap: "Childcare services inside the Singapore planning-area boundary"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = planning_area, fill = "#f5f7fa", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = childcare, color = "#c43c39", size = 0.35, alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Childcare centres follow Singapore's populated urban footprint",
    subtitle = paste(format(nrow(childcare), big.mark = ","), "service locations")
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

## Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test

The null hypothesis is CSR. Values of the Clark–Evans ratio (R<1) indicate shorter nearest-neighbour distances than expected under CSR; (R>1) indicates a more regular pattern. The CDF edge correction is suitable for the non-rectangular Singapore window.

```{r}
#| label: clark-evans-test

ce_sg <- clarkevans.test(
  childcare_ppp,
  correction = "cdf",
  alternative = "clustered"
)

ce_result <- data.frame(
  Area = "Singapore",
  `Clark-Evans R` = round(unname(ce_sg$statistic), 3),
  `p-value` = format.pval(ce_sg$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
  Decision = ifelse(ce_sg$p.value < 0.05, "Reject CSR", "Do not reject CSR"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(ce_result, caption = "Clark–Evans test with CDF edge correction")
```

**Answer.** (R=) **`r round(unname(ce_sg$statistic), 3)`** with **`r format.pval(ce_sg$p.value, eps = 0.001)`**, so the childcare pattern is significantly clustered relative to CSR. This is not evidence that centres attract one another; population, housing estates, zoning, and service demand are plausible spatially varying drivers.

## Kernel density estimation

`bw.diggle()` selects a data-driven fixed bandwidth. An adaptive KDE is also estimated: it uses narrower kernels where points are dense and wider kernels in sparse areas. Both surfaces are expressed as estimated centres per square kilometre.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-kde

fixed_bandwidth <- bw.diggle(childcare_ppp)

fixed_kde <- density(
  childcare_ppp,
  sigma = fixed_bandwidth,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

adaptive_kde <- adaptive.density(
  childcare_ppp,
  f = 0.15,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

fixed_grid <- as.data.frame(fixed_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = paste0("Fixed KDE (h = ", round(fixed_bandwidth), " m)"))

adaptive_grid <- as.data.frame(adaptive_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = "Adaptive KDE")

kde_grid <- bind_rows(fixed_grid, adaptive_grid)
```

```{r}
#| label: kde-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Fixed and adaptive estimates of childcare-centre intensity"
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5

ggplot(kde_grid, aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = planning_area, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.08, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(planning_area), datum = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", trans = "sqrt", na.value = NA) +
  labs(
    fill = "Estimated centres\nper km²",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: kde-peak
#| include: false

peak_cell <- fixed_grid[which.max(fixed_grid$value), ]
peak_point <- st_as_sf(peak_cell, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 3414)
peak_area <- st_join(peak_point, planning_area["PLN_AREA_N"], join = st_within)$PLN_AREA_N[1]
```

**Answer.** The fixed-bandwidth surface peaks in **`r tools::toTitleCase(tolower(peak_area))`**. The fixed surface is easier to compare across the island; the adaptive surface retains sharper local peaks in dense estates and smooths more aggressively in sparse peripheral areas. KDE measures concentration of facilities, not accessibility or demand satisfaction.

## Planning-area comparison

The course guide compares Punggol, Tampines, Choa Chu Kang, and Jurong West. Counts and area-standardised densities show why raw totals alone can mislead.

```{r}
#| label: planning-area-summary

focus_names <- c("PUNGGOL", "TAMPINES", "CHOA CHU KANG", "JURONG WEST")

childcare_with_area <- st_join(
  childcare,
  planning_area["PLN_AREA_N"],
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE
)

focus_summary <- planning_area |>
  filter(PLN_AREA_N %in% focus_names) |>
  mutate(Area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(PLN_AREA_N, Area_km2) |>
  left_join(
    childcare_with_area |>
      st_drop_geometry() |>
      count(PLN_AREA_N, name = "Centres"),
    by = "PLN_AREA_N"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `Centres per km²` = Centres / Area_km2,
    Area_km2 = round(Area_km2, 2),
    `Centres per km²` = round(`Centres per km²`, 2)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(`Centres per km²`))

kable(
  focus_summary,
  col.names = c("Planning area", "Area (km²)", "Centres", "Centres per km²"),
  caption = "Childcare provision in the four focus planning areas"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: local-clark-evans

make_local_ppp <- function(area_name) {
  boundary <- planning_area |> filter(PLN_AREA_N == area_name)
  local_points <- childcare[lengths(st_within(childcare, boundary)) > 0, ]
  local_xy <- st_coordinates(local_points)
  ppp(
    local_xy[, 1], local_xy[, 2],
    window = as.owin(st_union(boundary)),
    checkdup = FALSE
  )
}

local_tests <- lapply(c("CHOA CHU KANG", "TAMPINES"), function(area_name) {
  local_ppp <- make_local_ppp(area_name)
  test <- clarkevans.test(local_ppp, correction = "cdf", alternative = "clustered")
  data.frame(
    `Planning area` = tools::toTitleCase(tolower(area_name)),
    Centres = npoints(local_ppp),
    `Clark-Evans R` = round(unname(test$statistic), 3),
    `p-value` = format.pval(test$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()

kable(local_tests, caption = "Local Clark–Evans tests")
```

Tampines has more centres, while Choa Chu Kang has greater centres-per-area density because its boundary is much smaller. Both local (R) values are below 1 and statistically significant, so clustering is present within each planning area rather than being only an island-wide effect.

## Conclusion

The nearest-neighbour and KDE results agree: childcare services are not distributed uniformly. The strongest fixed-KDE concentration is in Sengkang, and substantial local clustering remains in Choa Chu Kang and Tampines. These are descriptive first-order findings; a demand-adjusted study would add child population, capacity, transport access, and housing density.
